bridge.Shipmates on the long voyage south: The coast of Wales slips away behind you, and the open sea lies ahead. Shall we get to know the men you'll be sailing with?
bridge.Through the ice to Cape Evans: Weeks go by, and the air grows colder every day. Then, one morning, you'd see something white and enormous on the horizon.
bridge.Building a home at Cape Evans: The anchor is down, and the black sand beach is waiting. Now there's a whole house to build, and you can help.
bridge.Inside the wooden hut: The ship has gone, and the hut is finished. Let's step inside together, out of the wind.
bridge.Ponies, dogs and penguins: The stove is warm and the bread is baking. But you'll want to meet the other members of the expedition, the ones with four legs, and wings.
bridge.The long polar night: The days are growing shorter, very fast. Can you feel the long darkness coming?
bridge.The winter journey for an egg: In the middle of that dark winter, three men did something very strange. Would you have gone with them?
bridge.Spring, the plan and a rival: The three men are home, safe and warm. And soon, you'd see a thin line of gold on the northern horizon.
bridge.Two roads to the Pole: The plans are made, and the sledges are packed. Two teams, far apart, are setting off across the same white continent.
bridge.Five men on the high plateau: The last support team has turned for home. Now there are only five of them, and the high, quiet plateau ahead.
bridge.The long way home: They've reached the Pole, and seen the little tent. Now they must turn around and walk all the way back. We'll go very gently from here.
bridge.Found, remembered, and the hut today: The wind sweeps over the empty ice. So what happened to the men at the hut, and what would you find there today?

voor.Scott's great expedition did not leave: Picture yourself standing on a crowded quay, with coal dust in the air and flags flapping overhead.
voor.The Terra Nova was not new: You'd smell old timber, tar and whale oil as soon as you stepped aboard.
voor.Every inch of the deck was crammed: You'd have to climb over crates just to reach the rail.
voor.In 1910, almost nothing was known: You might think the maps were nearly complete. They were almost blank.
voor.The leader was a quiet, serious naval of: If you'd met him, you'd have noticed his steady, thoughtful eyes.
voor.Scott's wife was a sculptor: You'd find her studio full of clay, plaster and lively conversation.
voor.Out of eight thousand eager letters: You can imagine the piles of envelopes on his desk.
voor.On their first night at sea: You'd hear the clink of glasses in the little wardroom.
voor.Before they reached the ice: You'd sweat under a blazing sun, long before you felt the cold.
voor.Scientists and officers took turns: You'd come up from the stokehold black with coal dust.
voor.The chief scientist was a gentle doctor: You'd find him sketching birds at the rail, smiling quietly.
voor.One officer paid a large sum: You might think he'd expect special treatment. He didn't.
voor.In a little New Zealand harbour: You'd hear dogs barking and ponies stamping on the deck.
voor.The first iceberg they saw: You'd stand at the rail and stare, hardly believing your eyes.
voor.On Christmas Day 1910: You'd feel the sun on your face, at midnight.
voor.Curious penguins walked up: You'd see them waddle closer and tilt their heads to listen.
voor.The first thing the men saw: You'd see a thin plume of steam rising from a white mountain.
voor.Unloading the ship took days: You'd lose track of time in the never-ending daylight.
voor.The hut came from England: You'd sort through the numbered pieces with your cold fingers.
voor.The only sounds at the hut: You'd stand still and hear almost nothing at all.
voor.Late in the evening, the men sat outside: You'd find yourself a box, sit down and simply watch.
voor.When the ship sailed away: You'd watch her grow smaller and smaller on the horizon.
voor.The hut was divided in two: You'd hear voices from both sides of the wall of boxes.
voor.Scott's little corner held a bunk: You'd see him writing in his diary by lamplight.
voor.At the end of the hut, a young cook: You'd wake to the smell of fresh bread every morning.
voor.In the coldest place on Earth: You'd hear music drifting through the hut on dark evenings.
voor.The warmest room in the hut: You'd squeeze in there just to warm your hands.
voor.The expedition's ponies came: You'd hear them snorting and stamping in their stable.
voor.Oates grumbled about the ponies: You'd find him in the stable at midnight, with a lantern.
voor.The sled dogs slept curled up: You'd see little mounds in the snow, each one a sleeping dog.
voor.The little Adélie penguins always looked: You'd laugh every time one of them looked at you.
voor.At night, the men could hear seals singi: You'd lie in your bunk and listen to those strange, soft songs.
voor.Before winter came, the men hid: You'd see the black flag flapping above the snow.
voor.On the twenty-third of April: You'd watch the last sliver of sun slip below the horizon.
voor.The polar night was not always black: You'd step outside and see the sky ripple with green and pink light.
voor.Even in endless darkness: You'd know exactly what time it was by the smell of the meals.
voor.Three evenings a week, someone gave: You'd sit on a bench, mug in hand, and listen.
voor.Midwinter Day was the Antarctic Christma: You'd see little flags and candles everywhere you looked.
voor.Three men walked out into the polar nigh: You might think it was madness. They thought it was science.
voor.At Cape Crozier, they built: You'd pile stones and snow with your mittened hands.
voor.When they finally found the emperor peng: You'd hear the birds trumpeting in the darkness.
voor.When the sun came back in August: You'd feel a lump in your throat as the first light touched the hills.
voor.Bowers spent whole days weighing food: You'd see him bent over the scales, humming to himself.
voor.The Norwegians spent the winter: You'd find them warm, well fed and very cheerful.
voor.The Norwegians travelled on skis: You'd hear the dogs yelping with excitement as they set off.
voor.Out on the Barrier, they marched at nigh: You'd feel the snow crunch firmly under your boots.
voor.On Christmas Day, high on the glacier: You'd see his grin as he pulled it out of his bag.
voor.Inside the tent each evening: You'd hold your hands over the little stove and feel them tingle.
voor.Tired as they were, they stopped: You might think they'd leave everything heavy behind. They didn't.
voor.In the second winter, the empty bunks: You'd walk quietly past them, not wanting to disturb anything.
voor.Scott's son grew up to love nature: You might know his name: Sir Peter Scott, who loved birds all his life.
voor.The hut at Cape Evans still stands: If you could visit, you'd see their old jars and boots still on the shelves.

slot.The Terra Nova was not new: I've always had a soft spot for her.
slot.Out of eight thousand eager letters: Would you have written one too?
slot.The expedition's photographer called him: Have you seen any of his pictures?
slot.In the coldest place on Earth: Can you hear it, tinkling in the dark?
slot.The hut had its own newspaper: What would you have written in it?
slot.Bowers took a famous photograph: Have you ever seen that picture?
